elements.quote: This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.

elements.quote: Editorials, commentaries, opinion papers, conference abstracts, media reports, letters, bulletins, pre-prints, grey literature, non-English language studies, systematic reviews and meta-analyses were excluded from the search.
elements.reason: The abstract reports some exclusion details, but it does not clearly specify the full main inclusion and exclusion criteria.

elements.quote: a comprehensive search across PubMed and Embase databases was performed of peer-reviewed literature published from inception until June 2024.
elements.reason: The abstract identifies information sources (PubMed, Embase) and the search time frame (until June 2024).

The abstract provided does not specify methods used to present and synthesize the results.

elements.quote: The search yielded 2950 records, of which 15 met the inclusion criteria.
elements.reason: The abstract reports the total number of included studies (15) and describes study characteristics, but it does not report total participants.

elements.quote: The studies were carried out mainly in countries in Africa (53.3%)... and countries in Asia (26.7%)... The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%).
elements.reason: The abstract presents results relevant to included studies/interventions, but it does not clearly present results for main outcomes (and does not include number of studies/participants per outcome).
The abstract does not report whether a meta-analysis was conducted, nor any summary estimate with a confidence/credible interval.

elements.quote: The most used interventions for analyses were insecticide-treated bed nets (93.3%), IRS (80.0%), Seasonal Malaria Chemoprevention (33.3%) and Case management (33.3%).
elements.reason: No group comparisons or effect directions are described in the abstract; therefore the PRISMA item about direction of effect/favored group is not applicable based on the provided abstract text.
The abstract conclusion discusses implications, but it does not briefly summarize important limitations of the included evidence (e.g., risk of bias, inconsistency, imprecision).

elements.quote: The findings highlighted the need for country-specific analysis for malaria control optimization, the use of country-specific epidemiological and cost data in performing modelling analyses, performing cost sensitivity analyses and defining the perspective for the analysis, with an emphasis on subnational tailoring for data collection and analysis for more accurate and good quality results.
elements.reason: The abstract provides an interpretation and states implications for future modelling efforts.
The abstract evidence provided does not specify the primary source of funding.

elements.quote: Background Despite advances made in curbing the global malaria burden since the 2000s, progress has stalled, in part due to a plateauing of the financing available to implement needed interventions.
elements.reason: Provides context on external drivers (stalled progress/financing) but only partially describes the current state of knowledge and important uncertainties relevant to modeling for malaria optimization.

elements.quote: Models for malaria control optimization are used to disentangle the most efficient interventions or packages of interventions for inherently constrained budgets. This systematic review aimed to identify and characterise models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in limited resource settings and assess their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: Explains the need for the review by stating the problem context and explicitly the review’s purpose/need (identify/characterise models and assess strengths/limitations).
No evidence is provided describing similar systematic reviews, or explaining why a new review is needed when previous reviews exist (including updates/replications and citing prior reviews).

The review is about identifying/characterising optimization models for malaria control (a systematic review of models), and the retrieved evidence does not indicate an intervention-effect review where a mechanism of action of an intervention is required to be described.

The retrieved evidence does not report a logic model to show hypothesised relationships between intervention components and outcomes for complex interventions/delivery contexts; moreover, this is a systematic review of optimization models rather than an intervention delivery logic-model specification.

elements.quote: The research question for this review was ' Are there English-language publications in peer-reviewed scientific journals describing how models have been used to allocate resources for malaria interventions in limited resource settings?' The main aim of this review was to identify and characterize models for malaria control optimization for resource allocation in malaria control and elimination settings and to identify their strengths and limitations.
elements.reason: The review provides an explicit research question and a stated main aim (objective) for the systematic review.
No planned intervention comparisons using PICO (or an appropriate variant) are stated in the retrieved evidence.

elements.quote: Each record in the search were included if they met all of the following criteria: (1) Were scientific peer-reviewed journals written in English; (2) Were published before 30th June 2024; (3) Studies were included irrespective of the targeted geographical regions; (4) Studies were included irrespective of the population subgroups; (5) Studies containing an optimization model (mathematical or statistical); (6) All studies with human Plasmodium species; (7) Studies with two or more interventions; (8) Cost data were used in combination with the model outputs; (9) Outcomes/health benefits were clearly stated and/or measured.
elements.reason: The inclusion criteria specify several eligibility characteristics (e.g., optimization model type, human Plasmodium, interventions, cost data usage, outcomes/health benefits). However, they do not clearly specify eligible study designs, settings, or follow-up requirements as described by the criterion.

elements.quote: Each record in the search were included if they met all of the following criteria: (1) Were scientific peer-reviewed journals written in English; (2) Were published before 30th June 2024;

No evidence was provided describing whether the review distinguishes exclusion due to outcomes not measured versus outcomes results not reported.

elements.quote: A total of 9 (60.0%) studies used at least one source of country-specific epidemiologic or cost data or both for the transmission model parameterization, model calibration or economic analysis, while 6 (40.0%) studies used non-country-specific epidemiologic and cost data for the transmission model parameterization, model calibration or economic analysis. The country-specific data were sourced from district health information system (DHIS) databases, country level reports, NMCP reports, national malaria strategic plans, demographic and health survey (DHS) data, malaria indicator cluster survey (MICS) data, expert opinion and routine health system surveillance records [10, 11, 25, 28, 32, 34, 35, 37, 38]. elements.quote: This manuscript provides a systematic review of existing literature to identify models for malaria control optimization. However, the review has certain limitations, which are outlined below: The review did not include abstracts from scientific conferences or other scientific meetings, potentially omitting important modelling studies conducted by national malaria control programs (NMCPs) to inform resource allocation decisions. And so, although the findings from this review shows that there are relatively few published modelling studies or examples that incorporate cost constraints and describe how to optimize limited budgets, the findings from this manuscript may not fully represent the actual use of models for malaria control optimization worldwide. The absence of these studies from the review limits the comprehensiveness of the findings, suggesting a need for the development of additional approaches to better capture and reflect the full range of modelling activities being undertaken globally.
elements.reason: The Discussion includes a dedicated limitations section describing limitations of the review’s included evidence (e.g., exclusion of conference abstracts and potential omission of modelling studies), along with how this affects representativeness and comprehensiveness.
